A white man in his 30s with a 7-year history of severe, mechanical, low back pain and long-standing mental depression. Current medications include duloxetine hydrochloride, clonazepam, oxcarbazepine, fentanyl, sulpiride, zopiclone, omeprazole magnesium, and baclofen. Patient admitted to self-administering subcutaneous injections of meperidine, 100 mg 4 times per day, for the past 3 years, at different sites, including the deltoid areas and abdomen.

Large and deep, irregularly shaped, cutaneous ulcer on the dorsum of right forearm with necrotic tissue and muscle exposure at the base. Woody induration of skin on both forearms and abdominal region. Bilateral contracture of deltoid, triceps, and biceps muscles. Active and passive range of motion restricted at shoulders and elbows. No signs of joint inflammation.

- Laboratory Tests:
  - Elevated serum creatinine kinase (192 U/L; reference range, 0-174 U/L)
  - Normal complete blood cell count
  - Normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate
  - Normal antinuclear antibody
  - Normal rheumatoid factor
  - Normal aspartate aminotransferase
  - Normal alanine aminotransaminase
  - Normal aldolase levels
  - Normal serum electrophoresis
  - Negative culture specimens for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungal organisms

- Histopathology:
  Image Title: Wedge biopsy from indurated skin of abdominal region
  Image Description: Shows lobular panniculitis, subcutaneous fat lobules with necrotic adipocytes and dense inflammatory infiltrates composed mainly of foamy histiocytes. Severe fibrosis in deep dermis and subcutaneous septa. Foreign-body giant cells and macrophages with large, foamy cytoplasm present. No evidence of thrombosis or vasculitis. No polarizable foreign material identified.

- Muscle Biopsy:
  Deltoid muscle biopsy showed no muscle involvement

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Fibrosis and ulceration caused by meperidine
B. Post-injection granuloma
C. Factitial panniculitis
D. Meperidine-induced panniculitis

A patient in their 70s presented with syncope that occurred 7 days before admission without preceding signs or symptoms, followed by exertional fatigue. Medical history includes hypertension, heart failure, and aortic valve replacement surgery in 2020 (complicated by prosthetic valve thrombosis). Current medications: warfarin, furosemide, metoprolol succinate, and spironolactone.

Heart rate: 61 beats/minBlood pressure: 114/74 mm HgOxygen saturation: 96%Temperature: 36.6°CPhysical examination was unremarkable

- ECG findings:  • Regular sinus rhythm, heart rate 75 beats/min  • Prolonged PR interval (240 milliseconds)  • Prolonged QRS duration (170 milliseconds)  • Morris index in lead V1  • Notched and monophasic R-wave in V1  • Absent S wave in leads I and aVL  • Left axis deviation (-81°)- Echocardiogram findings:  • Ejection fraction: 28%  • Akinesia of middle and basal segments of inferior and inferoseptal walls  • Diffuse left ventricular hypocontractility- 24-hour Holter monitoring:  • Regular rhythm  • Mean heart rate: 77 beats/min  • No pauses initially noted

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Ventricular tachyarrhythmia (e.g., paroxysmal or sustained ventricular tachycardia)
B. Advanced conduction system disease (e.g., possible progression to complete heart block)
C. Complete heart block (trifascicular block)
D. Masquerading bundle-branch block (MBBB) with progression to advanced atrioventricular block

cases.case_text:
A white woman in her 20s with unremarkable medical and ocular history presented with decreased vision in her right eye. Symptoms began 4 days prior to presentation, when she was struck by lightning directly to the right forehead while hiking.

- Uncorrected visual acuity measured 20/50 OD and 20/20 OS- Pupils were symmetric, with no relative afferent pupillary defect- Initial anterior segment examination was normal with absence of cataract- Initial dilated fundus examination showed no apparent abnormalities in either eye- At 2 weeks: central macular thickening in fundus examination- At 7 weeks: mild posterior subcapsular cataract visible in right eye

Spectral-domain OCT findings:- Initial examination (4 days post-injury):   Image Description: Preserved foveal contour in both eyes without cystoid abnormalities. Right eye showed subtle irregularity of the outer retinal layers, most notable nasal to the fovea  - Two weeks post-injury:  Image Description: Intraretinal cystoid changes and subfoveal ellipsoid zone disruption in the right eye  - Seven weeks post-injury:  Image Description: Restoration of foveal contour with decreased cystoid abnormalities, small subfoveal hyporeflective space, and further loss of outer retinal layers in the nasal macula  - Four months post-injury:  Image Description: Persistent subfoveal hyporeflective space in the inner retina with interval restoration of subfoveal outer retinal structures

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Traumatic macular retinopathy
B. Photic or lightning-induced retinopathy
C. Electric injury-induced maculopathy
D. Lightning-induced retinopathy with delayed-onset cystoid macular abnormalities

A 40-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain and constipation. She had been evaluated 3 months earlier for 3-4 months of amenorrhea. She had a history of thyroid condition. During the previous evaluation, thyroid-stimulating hormone was undetectable, and she was prescribed methimazole. She continued to have amenorrhea and reported abdominal fullness and constipation.

Vital signs were unremarkable. Physical examination revealed a tender midline abdominal mass.

- Initial Tests:    * Point-of-care (POC) urine human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) test: negative    * Thyroid-stimulating hormone: undetectable    * Radioiodine thyroid uptake study was performed      - Follow-up Tests:    * Serum hCG: 74,503 mIU/mL    * Ultrasonography: Confirmed live intrauterine pregnancy at 24 weeks

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Intrauterine Pregnancy
B. Pregnancy at 24 weeks gestation
C. Intrauterine pregnancy with hyperthyroidism (gestational thyrotoxicosis)
D. Thyroid storm with concurrent pregnancy

A patient in their 60s presented to the emergency department with paroxysmal chest pain. The chest pain had occurred 5 times during the day, and each episode lasted 15 to 30 minutes.

On arrival, the patient's blood pressure and pulse rate were 106/52 mm Hg and 64 beats per minutes, respectively. Chest auscultation revealed normal breath and heart sounds with no murmurs.

- Laboratory Tests:
  • Hemogram, serum electrolyte levels, kidney and liver function tests, B-type natriuretic peptide and D-dimer levels were all within normal limits
  • Cardiac troponin I level was 25 ng/mL (normal, <0.023 ng/mL)

- ECG Findings:
  Image A Title: Initial ECG
  Image A Description: Revealed sinus rhythm, ST-segment elevation in leads III and aVR, Q wave in lead III, and ST-segment depression in leads I, II, aVL, aVF, and V2 to V6

  Image B Title: Repeated ECG (taken during recurrent chest pain on second day)
  Image B Description: Reveals sinus bradycardia (46 beats per minute), Q-wave amplitude deepening, ST-segment falling back to equipotential line, and T-wave inversion in lead III

- Coronary Angiography:
  Findings showed total occlusion of the right coronary artery (RCA) and subtotal occlusion of the left main coronary artery (LMCA)

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Unstable angina
B. Acute non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) with Aslanger pattern
C. Coronary artery disease with acute coronary syndrome
D. Unstable Angina due to Multi-Vessel Coronary Artery Disease

cases.case_text:
A man in his 40s with unilateral otomandibular syndrome (OMS) associated with severe temporal bone hypoplasia had undergone many mandibular and auricular reconstruction surgeries in childhood. He presented with a history of deep unilateral neck cellulitis. The first episode occurred in 2014 with no obvious cause. The second episode occurred in 2021, with discharge through the artificial ear canal. Two months after the second episode, the patient experienced another recurrence of neck cellulitis.

Discharge was noted through the artificial ear canal during the second episode of cellulitis.

- Imaging Studies:    1. Initial CT scan:       - Title: Axial Plane CT Scan       - Description: Showed collection in the right parapharyngeal space and neck collection. A hypodense lesion was noted in the middle ear.        2. Follow-up MRI and CT scan:       - Title: Contrast-Enhanced Coronal Plane MRI       - Description: Revealed a fistula originating from the middle ear       - Title: Axial plane diffusion-weighted MRI       - Description: Showed a hyperintense 23-mm lesion at the edge of the petrous bone        3. Surgical Findings:       - 2-centimeter mass found during drilling of the hypoplastic petrous bone       - Millimetric fistula at the tip of the mastoid running into the sternocleidomastoid muscle

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Petrous bone cholesteatoma
B. Cholesteatoma with secondary infection
C. Cholesteatoma with fistula formation
D. Congenital cholesteatoma with fistula formation in the setting of otomandibular syndrome
